m:trinity: Entry is with a timed ticket booked online at visittrinity.ie: basic entry to the Book of Kells Experience starts from €25 (price read on the official website, varies by time slot). Hours: Monday–Thursday 8:30am–6:30pm, Friday and Saturday 8:30am–7pm, Sunday 9am–6:30pm; in winter they may be shorter. In the Long Room almost all the books have been removed for the Old Library renovation (only the first four bays remain): you can still see the Book of Kells, but you can't photograph it. On Wednesday 14 October 2026 Trinity College is closed because of the national strike.
m:guinness: Open every day from 9:30am; according to one guide it closes, with last entry, at 5pm from September to June and at 6pm in July and August (to be confirmed on guinness-storehouse.com). Entry is by time slot, best booked online. The standard ticket with a pint costs from about €26 on weekdays to €30–36 at weekends; reduced from about €22 for students and over-65s. At the desk you can only pay by card.
m:kilmainham: It can only be visited on a guided tour, with a ticket bought online on the museum website or heritageireland.ie: tickets from other sites aren't valid. 2026 prices: adults €8, over-65s €6, students €4, families €20; under-12s go free but still need a ticket. The visitor centre is open 9:30am–5:15pm and the museum 10:30am–5:15pm; the last tour leaves earlier. Closed from 24 to 27 December. Arrive 15 minutes before your tour (30–40 minutes before for the last two of the day).
m:christ: 2026 prices from guides: adults €12, ages 13–17 and over-65s €10, children aged 2–12 €4, including the crypt. Hours: Monday–Saturday 9:30am–6pm in October and 9:30am–5pm from November; Sunday only in time slots (about 12:30–3pm and 4:30–6pm in October, 12:30–2:30pm from November). Last entry is 45 minutes before closing and the cathedral may close for services: hours to be confirmed on christchurchcathedral.ie.
m:patrick: Open Monday–Saturday 9:30am–5pm; on Sundays tourist access is very limited because of services (which are free). Adult entry €11.50 with audio guide, reduced about €9 (prices from guides, to be confirmed on stpatrickscathedral.ie). There are free guided tours Monday to Saturday.
m:temple: Free to walk around at any hour. By day it's quiet; in the evening and at weekends it's very crowded and beer and food prices are higher than elsewhere: to eat better, move a few streets away.
m:grafton: The street is always open. The park is free and normally closes at sunset (hours change with the season). On Sundays the shops open later.
m:archaeo: Free entry. Hours: Tuesday–Saturday 10am–5pm, Sunday and Monday 1–5pm; last entry recommended at 4:30pm. Closed on 25 and 26 December and Good Friday, on 24 December 10am–noon. There's no luggage storage: suitcases and large backpacks aren't allowed. Some rooms may close without notice.
m:merrion: Hours: Monday and Sunday 11am–5:30pm, Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday 9:15am–5:30pm, Thursday 9:15am–8:30pm. Audio guides are free. The permanent collection is normally free (the page I read doesn't say: to be confirmed on nationalgallery.ie). The square's garden closes at sunset.
m:epic: Open every day 10am–6:45pm (from 9am June to August), closed from 24 to 26 December. Online ticket €22 adults, €11 children, free under 6. Last entry at 4:30 or 5pm (the website gives both times): arrive earlier. From the centre it's about a 20-minute walk along the river.
m:phoenix: The park is open 24 hours a day (side gates roughly 7am–10:45pm, according to one guide). Dublin Zoo is open 9:30am–5:30pm in October, with last entry at 4:30pm (prices on dublinzoo.ie, not checked). Áras an Uachtaráin, the president's residence, can usually be visited on Saturdays (to be confirmed). In autumn the sun sets early: arrive while it's light.
vd:brother: A bright brunch spot with Middle Eastern influences on the north bank of the Liffey: shakshuka with house bread, cardamom French toast and a good flat white. At weekends there's a queue before opening.
vp:brother: Budget to mid-range: a brunch is roughly €12–16 (menu not seen). Saturday and Sunday walk-in only. Hours from an online listing, to be confirmed.
vd:queen: An Irish bakery-café opposite Dublin Castle: potato and onion pies, fruit tarts, scones and apple crumble, with tea or coffee. Great for breakfast or afternoon tea.
vp:queen: Budget to mid-range: a pastry with tea is around €8–12 (menu not seen). Hours from an online listing, to be confirmed.
vd:leo: The city's most famous fish and chips, open since 1913, a step from Christ Church: fried cod and chips to take away, eaten in the street or in a nearby park.
vp:leo: Budget: fish and chips is roughly €12–16 (menu not seen). Hours from an online listing, to be confirmed.
vd:brazen: Dublin's oldest pub, with a licence dating back to 1198: low wooden rooms, a courtyard and live traditional music in the evening. Irish stew, fish and chips and shepherd's pie.
vp:brazen: Mid-range: a dish is around €16–22 (menu not seen). The kitchen serves until 9pm; the pub stays open until late. Hours from the pub's website, to be confirmed.
vd:gallagher: A traditional Irish restaurant in Temple Bar, specialising in boxty, the filled potato pancake. There's also beef and Guinness stew and shepherd's pie, in a cosy setting.
vp:gallagher: Mid-range: a main course is around €18–24 (menu not seen); an online listing says «€30 or less» per person. Hours from OpenTable, to be confirmed.
vd:cornucopia: A long-standing vegetarian and vegan restaurant a short walk from Grafton Street: a counter with salads, soups, cakes and hot dishes of the day. A light break in the heart of the shopping area.
vp:cornucopia: Budget to mid-range: lunch is around €12–16 (an online listing says $20–30 per person, menu not seen). Hours from an online listing, to be confirmed.
vd:kaph: A specialty coffee bar on a side street near Grafton Street: carefully made espresso and filter coffee, plant milks and something to eat. A place for a quiet breakfast or a mid-morning break.
vp:kaph: Budget: a coffee with a pastry is around €6–9 (menu not seen). Hours from an online listing, to be confirmed.
vd:panem: A small Italian-French café opposite the Ha'penny Bridge, on the north bank: croissants, chocolate brioche, filled focaccia and soups, with Sicilian arabica coffee. Few tables, high quality.
vp:panem: Budget: breakfast is around €6–10 (menu not seen). According to an online listing it doesn't take cards: bring cash. Hours from that listing, to be confirmed.
vd:windingstair: A restaurant above a historic bookshop overlooking the river, with seasonal Irish cooking: smoked fish, cod with cheddar mash, bread pudding with whiskey sauce. Best to book in the evening.
vp:windingstair: Mid-range: starters around €14, mains around €25 (some prices read in a guide, undated). Hours from an online guide, to be confirmed.
cd:jameson: The historic distillery with a guided tour and whiskey tasting.
cd:patrickcat: Ireland's largest church, where Jonathan Swift was dean.
cd:castle: The State Apartments and the medieval tower in the heart of the city.
cd:teeling: The only distillery founded in Dublin in the last hundred years, with a tour and tasting.
cd:dublinia: Vikings and medieval Dublin, with a tower to climb.
cd:whiskeymus: A history of Irish whiskey with a tasting of three glasses.
cd:littlemuseum: A Georgian house with the city's history told by the guides.
cd:gpo: The story of the 1916 Rising in the post office where it began.
cd:writers: Joyce, Beckett, Wilde and Yeats in an 18th-century mansion.
